prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and quantum spin Hall state, and its first experimental observation as protected edge-channel conduction in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: B038 is the cleanest example on the shortlist of what the Physics Prize is for: an original prediction (Kane and Mele, the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall state) followed by an original, decisive experiment (Molenkamp's group, quantized edge conductance in HgTe wells). The result was verified independently over about two decades in HgTe, InAs/GaSb, Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3-type materials, by transport and by ARPES, so it clears the bar of being experimentally verified. It also opened a door to materials with protected states that people could not previously see or exploit, and it connects to device concepts. The three-name configuration pairs two theorists with the experimentalist who actually made the first observation, which is the kind of 'who did the original work' account I would be comfortable defending.
statement.case_against: The credit is not clean. The HgTe quantum-well proposal that Molenkamp's experiment tested came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are outside the supplied names (Zhang is deceased), and the three-dimensional topological insulator discovery (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore and Balents; Hasan and the ARPES groups) is also outside the credit. If the committee cannot be 'absolutely sure' that these three people are the right ones, the prize should wait or be reframed. A second objection is that the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions and phases of matter already honoured the topological theme, so a reader may see this as the same ground a second time. Finally, the experimental side is the thinner half: one experimental group, with the 3D materials experiments left aside.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B038 first for the Z2 invariant and quantum spin Hall prediction followed by HgTe realisation, and flags that credit for the HgTe proposal and the 3D topological insulator lies partly outside the three names, and that it is unclear whether the citation should be narrow or broad.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case and with the caveat. I would resolve the scope question by keeping the citation narrow, to the quantum spin Hall state and the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator as predicted and first observed, and not claiming the whole 3D topological insulator field. That is the part where the original prediction and the original experiment line up in time and in people. The cost is that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang remain a real gap, and I do not think we should pretend the HgTe proposal was incidental, because Molenkamp's experiment was designed around it. I would rather say openly that this is a known attribution weakness than hide it.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B046 first as atomic physics at its most precise, where the clock opens genuinely new measurements, with Katori and Ye as a clean two-person credit and the 2005 and 2012 prizes covering neighbouring but not the same ground.
responses.response: I take this seriously, since B046 was my own second choice and the performance is verified in many national laboratories. Where I differ is on the margin: attribution is cleaner for B046, and I accept that is a real advantage over B038. But I do not think proximity to the 2005 comb prize is as small a problem as you suggest, because Ye shares that prize and the lattice clock leans on comb technology for the readout; and the priority history among Katori, Ye, Lemonde and Takamoto is not settled by what we have in front of us. I would not oppose B046 as the prize, but I think it should be judged on the same strict test of original work as B038, not given a pass because the credit looks tidy.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B046 first as an instrument that changes what can be measured, near 1e-18, with independent confirmation and a redefinition of the second pending, and also supports NV-centre sensing at third place.
responses.response: Instrument-driven arguments appeal to me too, and I share your view on NV sensing, where I credit Wrachtrup and Jelezko for the first observation. But I would separate 'instrument that changes what can be measured' from 'discovery'. The clock is an invention with verified performance and the committee has a clear rule that it counts. My reservation is about timing: a clock prize arguably gets stronger when the SI second is redefined, and I am not sure we gain anything by moving before that. I do not hold that as a veto, only as a reason I put B046 behind B038 in my ordering.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B036 first, arguing that defect-mediated 2D melting and the hexatic phase is a universal mechanism with lasting reach, long confirmed, and that recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I respect the argument that this is mature, but I have two serious problems with B036 as a prize. First, it sits right next to the 2016 prize to Kosterlitz and Thouless, who are themselves part of the dislocation-unbinding story, so the question of who did the original work is more tangled than for B038. Second, you note yourself that experiments and simulations show first-order melting in some systems and not others, so the universal scenario is not uniformly verified, and the experimental evidence (colloids, films) is more a later confirmation than an original experiment. That is closer to the second-discoverer case that the prize avoids. I would want a much clearer account of who first demonstrated the hexatic phase experimentally before I support it.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED B006 first, as a clean experiment that makes quantum physics visible and the standard architecture of superconducting processors, and notes his own proximity to the community.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED is a foundational architecture and I value that you flagged your own proximity. My concern is the attribution: four credited names for a three-person limit, with the 2004 theory proposal and the Wallraff and Schoelkopf experiments tightly intertwined, and with the transmon and Devoret-school work touching the 2025 prize. Two members rank it, and I cannot see us reaching a defensible three names without leaving out someone with a strong claim. If the committee did want to go there I would want the attribution question settled first. I also note that Chalmers has a strong superconducting-circuit community, so you and I are both close to this field, and that is another reason for me to be cautious in judging it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can justify omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (HgTe proposal) and the 3D topological insulator contributors from a prize built around B038.
Whether the 2016 topological phases prize makes B038 look redundant, or whether time-reversal-invariant topological insulators are distinct enough.
Whether B046 is better placed than B038 on attribution and whether to wait for the SI second redefinition before recognising lattice clocks.

Priority history within optical lattice clocks (Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Takamoto) and in twisted bilayer graphene (Bistritzer and MacDonald versus earlier flat-band work, and Cao's role) is only partly resolvable from the opening ballots.
statement.conflict_note: No personal conflict with any B038 candidate is apparent from my profile. I flag two institutional proximities. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague and champions B006 (circuit QED), a field where Chalmers has strong activity, and I have long-standing co-authors in Chalmers superconducting and device physics, so I would be cautious in judging B006 and would defer to others on it. Bernhard Mehlig is in the neighbouring Gothenburg physics department. I do not see these as requiring recusal on my preferred configuration.
